lead: After the sin of the golden calf, the first reading shows what remained between God and Moses: a tent outside the camp where the Lord spoke to him “face to face, as one speaks to a friend”, and a mountain where the Lord passed before him and proclaimed his name, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love. Moses’ prayer, “pardon our iniquity and our sin”, is answered with a renewed covenant. In the Gospel the disciples ask Jesus to explain the parable of the weeds, and he describes the harvest at the end of the age, when the righteous will shine like the sun. In both readings the patience of God is the ground of hope, and his justice is not forgotten.

r.h: The Lord used to speak to Moses face to face
set: The two passages come from after the golden calf (Exodus 32). God has said that his angel, but not he himself, will go with the people (33:2–3), and the people mourn. The “tent of meeting” described in 33:7–11 is not the grand tabernacle, which has not yet been built; it is a simple tent that Moses pitches outside the camp, a place of prayer and of seeking the Lord’s will.

Chapter 34 tells of the renewal: Moses cuts two new tablets and goes up the mountain again, and the Lord comes down in the cloud. The words proclaimed in verses 6–7 are among the most quoted in the Old Testament, repeated in Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 103:8, Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2.
str: 33:7–8: Moses’ tent outside the camp; the people watch him go.
33:9–11: the pillar of cloud, the Lord speaking with Moses face to face; Joshua stays.
34:5–7: the Lord descends, proclaims his name and his merciful character.
34:8–9: Moses bows and prays for forgiveness and for the Lord to go with them.
34:28: forty days and forty nights; the words of the covenant written on the tablets.
kw: A place where God and his people meet. Because it is outside the camp, the people must go out from their own tents to seek the Lord, and everyone who seeks him may go (33:7).

A Hebrew idiom for direct and friendly speech. The Lord says a little later in the same chapter that no one can see his face and live (33:20), so “face to face” describes closeness, not sight of God’s being.
The first two of the attributes of the Lord that the Jewish tradition calls the thirteen attributes of mercy. “Merciful” is from the word for womb, reḥem: the tenderness of a mother.
Faithful, covenant love that does not give up. It is the quality in God that most often makes the covenant possible after the people’s failure.
vv: Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.
This is the phrase that gives Moses his place among the prophets. In Numbers 12:8 the Lord says of Moses that he speaks with him directly, not in riddles.
The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,
God defines himself. He begins with mercy, not with power. This description is the foundation of the whole Old Testament’s hope in forgiveness.
keeping steadfast love for the thousandth generation,
God’s love reaches to a thousand generations, while his visiting of sin reaches only to three or four (v. 7). The balance is on the side of mercy.
Although this is a stiff-necked people, pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance.

God had called them a stiff-necked people (33:3, 5), and Moses uses the same word as a reason for God to go with them: because they are so weak they need God more. He includes himself in the sin: “our iniquity”.
ch: The Church reads God’s self-description in Exodus 34 as the root of everything she says about divine mercy. The Catechism presents Moses, who spoke to the Lord face to face as to a friend, as a model both of contemplative prayer and of intercession (CCC 2576–2577). It treats this same self-revelation of the Lord as “merciful and gracious” when it speaks of God’s mercy and love (CCC 210–211).

r.h: Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field
set: Jesus has told the parable of the weeds sown among the wheat (13:24–30): the householder’s servants want to pull up the weeds, but he says to let both grow together until the harvest. Now Jesus leaves the crowds, goes into the house, and explains it privately to his disciples. This is the second parable in the chapter with an explanation, after the sower (13:18–23).

The weeds were probably darnel, a plant that looks like wheat until it ripens. The parable answers a question early Christians asked and we still ask: if the kingdom has come, why is there still evil in the field?
str: v. 36: the disciples ask for an explanation.
vv. 37–39: the interpretation of each figure: the sower, the field, the good seed, the weeds, the enemy, the harvest and the reapers.
vv. 40–42: the end of the age: the Son of Man sends angels to collect the causes of sin and the evildoers.
v. 43: the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
kw: A weed that looks like wheat. Pulling it up early would destroy the wheat. The point is patience, not indifference to evil.
Literally “stumbling blocks”. They are removed from the kingdom, not individual weak people, but the things that make others fall.
The close of the present age, when God’s purpose is completed. The expression is characteristic of Matthew (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20).
vv: The field is the world, not only the Church. Jesus sows his Word in the whole world, and the good seed is “the children of the kingdom”.
Just as the weeds are collected and burned up with fire, so will it be at the end of the age.
Judgment belongs to God and comes at the end. Until then the disciples’ task is not to uproot the weeds but to grow as good wheat.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
An echo of Daniel 12:3, where those who lead many to righteousness shine like the stars. The end of the story is light, and the Father’s kingdom is home.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in every member of the Church, the weeds of sin are still mixed with the good wheat of the Gospel until the end of time (CCC 827). It adds that the Church is therefore holy, yet always in need of purification, and follows the way of penance and renewal (CCC 827). The Church’s teaching on the last things quotes the same Gospel: Jesus solemnly proclaims that he will send his angels, and they will gather all who do evil (CCC 1034). St Augustine used the parable to teach that in this age the good and the bad are mixed in the Church and in the world (in substance); only God can sort them, and so we are to judge no one beforehand.

qa: Does God punish children for the sins of their parents (Exodus 34:7)?

No. The Bible itself corrects this reading. Ezekiel 18 says plainly that the child will not bear the guilt of the parent, and Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids it in the courts. Exodus 34:7 means that sin has long consequences in families and communities, as hatred, violence and addiction pass from one generation to the next. It also says that God’s love reaches a thousand generations, far beyond the reach of sin.
study: God describes himself first as “merciful and gracious”. When I think of God, do I begin with mercy or with fear?
Jesus teaches patience with the weeds. Where in my family or parish am I tempted to “pull up the weeds” instead of praying and waiting?
